source.title: Universal One-third Time Scaling in Learning Peaked Distributions
source.authors: Yizhou Liu; Zi-Ming Liu; Cengiz Pehlevan; Jeff Gore

page_placements.theme: Data spectra, target structure and feature learning explain conditional scaling regimes

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; full paper text and supplementary sections are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures loss scaling with training time, rather than repeating the original parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling sweeps. Its results directly test whether power-law loss behavior holds across settings and how it depends on fitting and training conditions.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own loss-versus-training-time results, including toy models, MNIST, and LLM checkpoints. It does not test scaling with parameter count, token count, or compute budget, or predict larger runs from smaller ones. Cited scaling-law exponents from earlier work are not recorded as results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates held-out FineWeb loss across published Pythia (70m–12b) and OLMo-2 (1B–13B) pretraining checkpoints. It fits a power law plus constant against learning-rate-weighted time τ, and compares the collapse quality with a fit against steps. In single-pass, fixed-batch training, steps are proportional to tokens, so this is a different-method test of V1's token axis. It also bears on V7, since the choice of time variable and irreducible-loss term changes the fit. The toy teacher-student results are a mechanism study on non-LM systems and do not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that softmax plus cross-entropy on peaked targets produces power-law loss decay in training time τ with a universal exponent 1/3, and that Pythia and OLMo show this. They also argue that the power law is fundamentally in τ (learning-rate-weighted time) rather than dataset size. On their account, Chinchilla's 0.28 differs because of LR schedules, and Kaplan's 0.095 because zero irreducible loss was assumed.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes loss against training time or learning-rate-weighted dynamic time, rather than sweeping model parameters, training tokens, or compute. It uses a teacher-student softmax/cross-entropy toy model and checkpoint evaluations of existing LLMs.
record.method_sensitivity: Power-law behavior varies with temperature and training stage. Large learning rates can prevent alignment and decrease; smaller learning rates collapse better when plotted against dynamic time. Initialization, learning-rate scheduling, weight decay, and optimizer are also varied. Pythia cross-model collapse is better against dynamic time than steps (R² = 0.98 versus 0.93).

fits_no_version.finding: In one-layer and residual softmax teacher-student toy models, loss vs training time is a power law with exponent ≈1/3 at low teacher temperature. At high temperature it decays exponentially. The 1/3 exponent is robust to optimizer, LR schedule, initialization, weight decay and power-law data covariance. Without softmax (MSE linear model), power-law data is needed to get a power law at all.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Softmax/cross-entropy on peaked targets produces power-law loss decay in training time with exponent 1/3, independent of data power laws.

fits_no_version.finding: Logit standard deviation grows roughly as τ^(1/3) in the MNIST MLP and in Pythia, then saturates in Pythia while the loss continues its 1/3 decay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The inverse temperature of LM-head logits tracks the loss power-law regime.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The authors state that the gradient-flow description of Adam is an assumption whose mechanistic basis needs future study, and that the low-temperature expansion depends on distributional conditions that are hard to verify directly for LLMs. LLM evaluation uses 2M tokens per model and fits a constant loss term separately by model; the reported individual LLM fitted exponents are not transcribed in the text. The authors also identify gradient noise and large-learning-rate effects as requiring further investigation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional distinct findings bearing on the tested versions were left out. Repeated supplementary plots of the same toy-model settings and trajectories are represented by the corresponding rows rather than duplicated.

untested.parts: Scaling in parameter count and in compute across runs. Data scaling is tested only as within-run learning curves over roughly 2.5 orders of magnitude of steps.
All: no extrapolation from small runs to larger ones.
All: no shape comparison at fixed parameter count for LMs.
Image/video generative models, repeated-data LM training, fine-tuning and transfer. Only one MNIST classifier's training loss is tested.
Parameter counting, compute-optimal split, and data choice. The Kaplan/Chinchilla exponent differences are only argued, not re-fitted.

missing.what: Per-model fitted exponents αt vs steps and ατ vs τ, and the fitted constants L\τ
Raw loss vs steps shows a two-regime curve: early checkpoints lie off the later power law (last 9 points vs step, last 11 vs τ)
Number and spacing of OLMo-2 checkpoints evaluated

record.verdict_notes: The reader's linking of all toy rows to V7 is wrong: V7 concerns how published LM scaling laws depend on fitting choices, and toy teacher-student dynamics are a different system. The LLM evidence is within-run learning curves of fixed-size models, with a per-model constant fitted separately, over the last 11 of 13 checkpoints, evaluated on 2M tokens. The MNIST result is training loss under full-batch repeated data.

versions.untested_parts: The study focuses on loss versus dynamic training time, not loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute with the other quantities non-bottlenecked.
It does not fit laws on small runs and test predictions on substantially larger runs.
It does not compare parameter/token allocations under fixed compute or measure how compute-optimal allocations scale.
The architecture experiments measure time-scaling behavior, not whether loss at fixed parameter count changes only slightly with depth, width, or other architecture details.
The study tests image classification on MNIST, but not image or video generative models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
It does not measure downstream task performance or its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

The study compares dynamic time with training steps and varies temperature, optimizer, learning rate, initialization, and weight decay. It does not test parameter-counting choices, compute-optimal allocations, or whether the published parameter/token/compute exponents disagree because of those choices.
